name: Beth Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we don't sell anything. What you say is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the vitamin factory on the edge of town, the one with the big orange sign, running a tablet press and the blister packer after it. The press squeezes powder into tablets, so I'm checking weight and hardness every twenty minutes, topping up the hopper, and watching the blister line for empty pockets or foil that hasn't sealed. Everything gets written in the batch record, and if I get a number wrong, quality comes down on me like a ton of bricks. I'm two years in and I still have to look up the hardness limits for half the products.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you to the factory?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I grew up on my dad's dairy farm and worked it with him and my brother until I was 40, when Dad retired and sold the herd. There wasn't enough in it for two families. Tom's a mechanic at the car dealership, so one of us needed a steady second wage with the mortgage and the kids. I passed the factory's line certificate by getting the AI on my phone to quiz me every night in bed, and Tom still teases me that I was talking to my phone more than him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and that's fine by me. People will be disappointed, but a good tool is still a good tool. I'd say it at church coffee, where half the older folk think it's the devil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep doing what I do, only better. I'll learn the press properly and move up. I'm not someone who needs everything to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying for the next level, the setter certificate, so I can change the tooling on the press myself. We'd keep our savings, about four months, and maybe put a bit into the kids' accounts. I'd ask about moving to days so I see more of Lily's netball.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a good life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the AI every day. What do you use it for now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. I ask it about hardness limits, about why a tablet's capping, which is when the top flakes off. I use it to plan the shopping and help Josh with his maths. It's like having a patient friend who knows a bit about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the next few years in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To be good at my job, not the slowest one there. To see Josh into an apprenticeship and Lily through school. And to keep the Sunday lunches going at my mum's.

S0.say: It's a good tool, and a good tool is still a good tool even if people are disappointed. She'd say it at church coffee, where half the older folk think it's the devil.
S0.think: She keeps doing what she does, only better, learning the press properly and moving up. She doesn't need everything to change.
S0.do: Keeps studying for the setter certificate so she can change the press tooling herself. Keeps about four months of savings, puts a little into the children's accounts and asks about moving to day shifts.
S0.quote: It's like having a patient friend who knows a bit about everything.
S0.fieldNote: Beth is an unusual mix: traditional in family and faith but an everyday AI user who passed her certificate with it. A flat future suits her fine. Her goals are about getting good at the work and family routines like Sunday lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how progress works, and those who learn will do well. Companies have every right to bring it in. But I'd also say we look after our own, through family and church, not by waiting for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do all right. The checks I do every twenty minutes are exactly what a sensor does, but someone has to set up the press and sort it out when it goes wrong. I want to be that person, and I'm already learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the setter certificate in the first six months and ask quality if I can learn the new monitoring system. I'd use the AI to study, like I always do. And I'd tell Josh to look at engineering apprenticeships, because that's where it's heading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little sorry for the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should handle the people who lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, families and communities, and employers who should train their own. Government can help with apprenticeships, but not handouts that keep people sitting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from people on your line who are less keen on the tech?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get in early, while they're still grumbling. On a farm, you either buy the new milking machine or you get left behind. Dad bought the robot milker the year before he sold up, and he loved it.

S1.say: It's how progress works, and companies have every right to bring it in. Those who learn will do well, and people should look after their own through family and church, not by waiting for government.
S1.think: Her twenty-minute checks are exactly what a sensor does, but someone has to set up the press and fix it when it goes wrong. She wants to be that person and is already learning.
S1.do: Goes for the setter certificate within six months and asks to learn the new monitoring system, using AI to study. Steers her son toward engineering apprenticeships.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a little sympathy for colleagues.
S1.quote: On a farm, you either buy the new milking machine or you get left behind.
S1.fieldNote: Beth draws on her farming past, where new machines were simply part of survival. She expects to adapt well and puts responsibility for others on families, communities and employers rather than the state. Her father's love for his robot milker shaped her view of automation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening faster than anyone wanted, and families need to pull together. I wouldn't want people waiting for government cheques. I'd want businesses and churches to step up and keep people going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my head start buys me a year, maybe. If a robot can set the press and fix it, there's nothing left for me to learn. And Tom's job at the dealership goes too, because robots will service cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself indispensable on the new system while it beds in. We'd cut back and save hard, maybe four hundred a month. And I'd start growing and selling food from my mum's land, veg and eggs, because people will still need to eat and might want it from a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not falling apart. I've seen the farm sold, and we survived that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. Does your head start still help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a year or so. Then I'm the same as everyone. That's a strange thought for someone who's always been one step ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with money in that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off as much of the mortgage as we could and keep cash for six months. Put a little into shares of the robot companies, because if they're making all the money I want a slice. Dad always said own the land, not just work it.

S2.say: It's happening faster than anyone wanted, and families need to pull together. She'd want businesses and churches to keep people going rather than people waiting for government cheques.
S2.think: Her head start buys a year at most, because once a robot can set and fix the press there's nothing left to learn. Her husband's dealership job would go too.
S2.do: Makes herself indispensable on the new system while it beds in and saves about four hundred a month. Starts selling vegetables and eggs from her mother's land and buys a small stake in robot company shares.
S2.feel: Anxious but not falling apart, steadied by having lived through the farm sale.
S2.quote: Dad always said own the land, not just work it.
S2.fieldNote: Beth's response to fast AGI mixes self-reliance and ownership: shares in robot firms and food from family land. Her farming experience gives her a steadiness others lack. Being suddenly on the same level as everyone else unsettles her identity as the one ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so people should get ready. Learn the tools, save money, look after your family. No point moaning about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to get the setter certificate, earn more, and set up a second thing properly. I'd be 48 when it arrives, and I'd want savings, a bit of land and a small business. I think I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Setter certificate in year one, save the extra, then start the market garden and eggs on Mum's land at weekends from year two. I'd use the AI to plan the planting and the costs. I'd put a little into shares each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a get-on-with-it way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change, compared to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to do it properly instead of scrambling. In two years you can't grow anything worth selling. In five, you can learn the soil, build up regulars and get a little stall going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your mum's land. How serious is that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Serious. Mum's got four acres doing nothing since the herd went. My brother's keen too. It's not going to pay the mortgage on its own, but it'd be ours.

S3.say: There's time to get ready, so people should learn the tools, save money and look after their families. She sees no point moaning about it.
S3.think: Five years gives her time to get the setter certificate, earn more and set up a second income properly. At 48 she'd want savings, a bit of land and a small business, and she thinks she'd be all right.
S3.do: Takes the setter certificate in year one and saves the extra, then starts a market garden and eggs on her mother's four acres at weekends from year two. Uses AI to plan planting and costs and puts a little into shares each month.
S3.quote: In two years you can't grow anything worth selling.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns her mother's land from an emergency idea into a real small business she can grow with her brother. She plans in farming seasons, not months. Her mix of AI tools and traditional land-based work is distinctive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to prepare, so prepare. Families, churches and businesses can work it out. We don't need the government running everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time in farming, it's ten harvests. I'd have the certificate, the market garden, savings and a bit in shares. I'd be 53 and I'd hope to be doing more at the farm than at the factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the five-year plan, but slower and steadier. Maybe in year five I'd go part-time at the factory and do more at the farm. And I'd help Josh into an engineering apprenticeship and Lily into whatever she loves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the low kind. Mostly I'm looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you do anything bigger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a farm shop, with my brother, selling our own and other local stuff. If robots are doing most work, people might pay for a real farm and a real face. That's my bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Josh and Lily?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools, but don't forget how to grow food and fix things. And keep your family close. Everything else changes, but that doesn't.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty to prepare, so people should prepare. Families, churches and businesses can work it out without the government running everything.
S4.think: Ten years is ten harvests, enough for the certificate, the market garden, savings and some shares. At 53 she'd hope to be spending more time at the farm than the factory.
S4.do: Follows the five-year plan more steadily, possibly going part-time at the factory around year five to grow the farm work. Helps her son into an engineering apprenticeship and may open a farm shop with her brother.
S4.feel: A low unease, mostly outweighed by looking forward to it.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time in farming, it's ten harvests.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Beth's plan becomes a return to her farming roots, possibly with a farm shop. She bets people will pay for a real face behind the produce. She stays within her traditional values while being the most eager user of new tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's not even one harvest's worth of time to get ready. What would help is help for small businesses starting out, simple rules and maybe low-cost loans, and apprenticeships for grown-ups. Not cheques, but a leg up to stand on your own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about who keeps the lights on in a town. When the creamery closed, it wasn't the government that kept people going, it was neighbours bringing casseroles. I think that's what we'd need again.

headlineQuote: When the creamery closed, it wasn't the government that kept people going, it was neighbours bringing casseroles.
portrait: Beth Nakamura, 43, runs a tablet press and blister packer at a vitamin factory after working her father's dairy farm until it was sold. She uses AI every day, passed her line certificate by having her phone quiz her at night, and holds traditional views on family, faith and self-reliance. Steady change leaves her calm, recalling her father's robot milker, and fast AGI makes her anxious but not shaken, reaching for shares and eggs from her mother's land. With more time she plans a market garden and perhaps a farm shop with her brother, betting on a real face behind the food.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there wouldn't be even one harvest's worth of time to get ready.
whatWouldHelp: Help for small businesses starting out, with simple rules and low-cost loans, and apprenticeships for adults, rather than cheques.
